instructional_purpose: Introduces the class of nouns that decline with a reduced set of case exponents and refuse nunation, and teaches the paired-trigger account that is supposed to decide membership. Organises the class into named subgroups (proper names, toponyms, two adjective templates, one plural template family) so the learner can recognise members on sight.

paired-trigger licensing: one semantic trigger plus one formal trigger

state adjectives on the فعلان template
broken plurals of the صيغة منتهى الجموع family

linguistic_propositions.proposition: Membership in the reduced-paradigm class requires a semantic trigger (proper-name or adjective status) together with a formal trigger; either alone is insufficient.
A member of the class marks the genitive slot with fatha rather than kasra and carries no nunation in any case, as long as it stays indefinite and unannexed.
Broken plurals whose template places a long vowel before the final consonantal slot join the class on template evidence alone, without a separate semantic trigger.
Three-letter loan proper names stay fully declining; the lesson attributes this to shortness alone.

Several personal names presented as class members in the text-analysis section sit on templates that the lesson's own trigger chart never lists as formal triggers (an active-participle template and a فعيل template).
One toponym is assigned to the class on the ground of inherent feminine gender.
Ordinary Arabic proper names on common templates remain fully declining, so proper-name status is not by itself predictive.

instructional_purpose: Teaches the conditions under which the reduced-exponent class taught previously is suspended and the noun returns to the ordinary genitive exponent, and separates restoration of the case vowel from restoration of nunation. Adds a four-state summary of how one lexeme behaves across definiteness and annexation configurations.

linguistic_propositions.proposition: Prefixing the definite article suspends the reduced paradigm, so the genitive slot takes the ordinary vowel.
Serving as the first term of an annexation suspends the reduced paradigm for the same reason.
Neither operation restores nunation in prose, because both render the noun definite and nunation belongs to indefiniteness.
Verse may restore nunation to a class member when metre demands it; this licence does not extend to prose.
The second term of an annexation keeps the reduced paradigm if it independently qualifies, since the annexation definitises only the first term.
A following relational (nisba) adjective is claimed to behave like annexation and to restore the ordinary genitive vowel to the preceding proper name.
Illustrations attach the definite article directly to proper toponyms to demonstrate suspension.
A shortened noun ending in a non-vocalisable alif is listed as a member of the reduced-exponent class in its indefinite state.

linguistic_propositions.proposition: When singular and annexed, members of the set expone nominative, accusative and genitive with three distinct long vowels instead of the ordinary short vowels.
Annexation to the first-person singular clitic cancels the long-vowel series and the noun reverts to ordinary short exponents.
Unannexed occurrences decline like ordinary nouns and can carry nunation; dual and plural forms use their own regular exponents.
The possessive member of the set occurs only annexed to an overt noun and never takes a pronominal clitic.
The feminine counterpart of the possessive member is described as invariable, although the lesson's own illustrations show it with three different final vowels.
The long-vowel exponents are the historical reflex of a weak final radical that surfaces only under annexation.
The mouth-word member is listed with the set although its unannexed alternate lexeme, and the conditions for using it, are not supplied.

linguistic_propositions.proposition: A noun ending in a glide preceded by kasra shows a visible exponent only in the accusative when definite; nominative and genitive exponents are covert.
The same class, when indefinite, deletes the final glide in nominative and genitive and keeps it in the accusative.
A noun ending in a non-vocalisable alif has covert exponents in all three cases, so the three forms are homographic and only context disambiguates.
The indefinite of that alif-final class carries one nunation shape irrespective of case.
A noun ending in alif plus hamza carries all three exponents visibly and declines like an ordinary noun.
When a suffix beginning with alif is attached, the final hamza of the extended class may shift to a glide.
The dual of an extended-class noun is given with two alternates, without stating which historical source of the hamza selects which alternate.
Class membership can be decided by asking whether the final letter can carry a damma.
The class boundary is drawn against ordinary nouns ending in a doubled glide, which are not members despite the similar spelling.

linguistic_propositions.proposition: A closed range of nominal categories keeps one surface shape in every syntactic position.
A fixed-form noun still occupies a case slot; the convention records the invariant final vowel together with the slot it occupies.
The interrogative meaning 'which' varies its ending when it heads an annexation, unlike the rest of its category.
The dual demonstratives alternate shape between the nominative and the other two cases, and grammarians disagree whether that alternation is inflection or two separate fixed shapes.
Non-human plural antecedents take the feminine singular relative rather than the masculine plural relative.
Each fixed adverb carries a lexically specified final vowel that must be learned with the item.
Fixed-form nouns never take nunation.
The categories are fixed because of their origin as particles or their special history.

instructional_purpose: Introduces four discourse-level particles that manage attention, topic structure, presentation and surprise, and shows how each is recognised structurally rather than semantically. Anchors them in formal registers such as petitions, court speech and narrative turning points.

the topic-comment frame and its obligatory linking prefix on the comment

linguistic_propositions.proposition: The attention particle precedes a statement to alert the addressee and frequently combines with the emphatic nominaliser for reinforced emphasis.
The topic-setting particle requires the linking prefix on the following comment; omission is ungrammatical.
The presentative element fuses with deictic bases to yield the demonstrative series and also stands independently in fixed presentative formulas.
The surprise use appears only after a coordinating or consequential prefix and is followed by a nominal rather than a verb, whereas the conditional use is clause-initial and takes a verb.
The surprise use is not followed by a conditional apodosis, which is offered as a further diagnostic.
The attention particle and a homographic negated subordinator are distinguished only by gemination on the second letter.
These particles add emphasis and structure without altering the case assignment of what follows them.

linguistic_propositions.proposition: The specification noun is accusative, indefinite, and follows the element whose vagueness it resolves.
Specification splits into a subtype whose specified element is overtly stated and a subtype whose specified element is only implied by the construction.
After the mid-range numerals the specifier is singular rather than plural.
In a measure phrase, both the measure word and the specifier are accusative, and the measure word is labelled an adverbial complement.

The non-interrogative quantifier is illustrated with an accusative specifier, whereas the standard rule assigns its complement the genitive and reserves the accusative for the interrogative counterpart.
One rule illustration pairs a mid-range numeral with a plural specifier, contradicting the singularity requirement stated two rules later in the same section.
A specifier is posited as elided for a comparative that has none on the surface.
Specification is distinguished from the circumstantial accusative by asking whether the noun answers 'in what respect' rather than 'in what state'.
The specifier is indefinite because it names a general domain rather than a particular referent.
